facts.claim: Gravity's pull on a falling climber, a rope or falling ice: standard gravity.

versions.note: Defined by ISO 80000-3; the real pull is about 0.5% greater at the poles than at the equator.

facts.claim: How hard snow holds a body sliding over it in ski clothing, the coefficient of kinetic friction: the game uses it for a climber sliding after a slip, and for a rope lying on the ground.

versions.note: Three fabrics on snow, a ski overall and two race suits, on a linear tribometer: dry friction, highest on the roughest fabric.

source.title: Nachbauer et al. 2016, Kinetic Friction of Sport Fabrics on Snow (Lubricants) → Abstract

facts.claim: The gradients, the rise over the run, on which the energy cost of walking was measured: from 0.45 m down to 0.45 m up for each metre across, about 24°.

versions.note: Ten runners on a treadmill, walking and running at gradients from −0.45 to +0.45.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking on the level costs, for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked, at the speed that makes it least.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking up the steepest gradient measured, +0.45, costs for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The energy walking down the steepest gradient measured, −0.45, costs for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked: a fifth of the way up it.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The least energy walking costs on any gradient, for each kilogram of body mass and metre walked: on a gentle way down, technique.walking-cost-least-gradient, half the level's.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The gradient on which walking costs least: 0.10 m down for each metre across, about 6°.

versions.note: The cost is reduced to its least at −0.10.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: Steeper than this gradient, up or down, walking works the muscles at the efficiency of their contraction, concentric up and eccentric down: the work against gravity is most of the cost, so each metre of height costs about the same however steep. The game takes it from 0.15 up, and from the steepest measured down.

versions.note: The mechanical efficiencies of walking and running above +0.15 and below −0.15 attained those of concentric and eccentric muscular contraction.

source.title: Minetti et al. 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes (J Appl Physiol) → Abstract

facts.claim: The power a fresh typical client at sea level, at a steady pace and carrying nothing, walks on, in watts for each kilogram they move: the body scales it by the capacity the altitude leaves, 60% at 5,000 m, and by the pack, and a step goes as fast as it pays for on the ground's gradient (technique.walking-cost-*). Fitted with the fastest walk and the ladder speeds so that a steady first crossing of the Icefall, drawn at 1/12 of its length (route.drawn-scale) with its walls and crevasses at life size, takes about 5 hours, the middle of the 3–7 the sources give: 4.8.

The fastest a climber walks in crampons, in metres a second, whatever power they have to spare: down a slope and on the flat their footing holds them to it, so their steps take less of their power and tire them less. Fitted with the walking power and the ladder speeds so that the way down the Icefall takes about 2.5 hours, the 4 from Camp 2 to Base Camp shared between the Icefall and the Western Cwm as the way up's 5 and 3 are: 2.8.

Up to this steepness a climber in crampons doesn't slip; steeper, the chance grows in a straight line to technique.slip-chance-steep at the steepest ground walked. Fitted to the Lhotse Face, about 30°, where a slip ends badly, and to the Icefall's 20° slopes, walked without a thought.

The chance a climber slips in a second of walking the steepest ground walked without a ladder at a whole stride, scaled by their speed against that so that a slow climber slips as often for each metre. Fitted so that a few slips come on a long steep stretch, each held by the rope when the climber is clipped: the lesson is the rope, not the footing.

How fast that fresh climber at sea level crosses a ladder laid flat over a crevasse, in metres a second. The ladders are drawn at life size on a section drawn at 1/12 (route.drawn-scale), so a ladder takes twelve times its real mountain minutes: fitted with the speeds up and down a wall so that the Icefall's twenty ladders, nine over crevasses and eleven up and down walls of 3 to 11 m, take about an hour and a half of the way up's hours together.

How fast that climber goes up a ladder stood against a wall, in metres a second; between flat and vertical, the speed falls in a straight line over the sine of the ladder's angle. Fitted with the crossing speed to the Icefall's hours.

How fast that climber comes down a wall a ladder stands against, in metres a second: three times as fast as up it, as down the fixed rope beside it (technique.down-a-fixed-rope asks how climbers go down one). Fitted with the crossing speed and the fastest walk to the Icefall's hours down, which go down 48 m of its walls and up 22.

The chance a climber slips in a second on a ladder, whatever its angle, scaled by their stride. Fitted so that a slip comes on about one crossing of the Icefall in five: a scare on the rope for a climber clipped in, and the 2012 fall for one who isn't.
On Everest, climbers who had climbed on another peak of Nepal before summit more often than those who hadn't, and die no less often.

versions.note: 67.6% against 61.5% summited in 2006–2019, an advantage that has about halved in 25 years; deaths, the descent's too, independent of experience. The database records earlier Nepalese and border peaks, not other mountains.

source.title: Huey et al. 2020, Mountaineers on Mount Everest: Effects of age, sex, experience, and crowding on rates of success and death (PLoS One) → Results

facts.claim: The share of the speed on a ladder and clipped to a fixed rope of a climber who has never used crampons, a jumar or a ladder, against one with alpine climbs behind them, whom the ladder speeds and the walking power are fitted to. Fitted so that such a climber, as fit as the typical client, takes the longest the sources give a first crossing of the Icefall, 7 hours against the middle's 5.

The same share for a climber who has climbed a 7,000 m or an 8,000 m peak. Fitted so that such a climber, as fit as the typical client, crosses the Icefall the first time in 4 hours, the shortest Alan Arnette's routes give it, and summits more often: they take less time on the ropes, not fewer risks (technique.experience-and-summits).

How far a cowstail reaches from the climber's harness to the fixed rope, in metres: how far from the rope they can clip, and how far past an anchor the rope lets them. Fitted so that a climber beside a ladder can reach the rope fixed along it.

How fast falling ice, an avalanche or a breaking snow bridge throws a climber it catches down the slope, in metres a second: a fall their rope holds if they're clipped. Fitted so that an unroped climber caught on a slope slides off it.

The fastest slide a climber can stop with the ice axe driven into the slope, in metres a second: self-arrest works in a slide's first moments or not at all. Fitted to the Lhotse Face, where a slip not stopped at once ends badly.
How far from their body a sliding climber can drive the ice axe into the slope, in metres: an arm and the axe. Fitted with the arrest speed to the Lhotse Face.

facts.question: At an anchor where one fixed rope ends and the next begins, in what order does a climber move their cowstails across, and are they ever clipped to neither rope?

How do climbers on the South route rig their cowstails: the jumar on one and a carabiner on the other, and how long is each, so how far can a climber reach to clip? The game gives a cowstail 0.8 m of reach.

How does a climber cross a ladder laid over a crevasse in the Icefall: clipped to what, stepping how in crampons, and how fast? The game crosses at 0.6 m/s at sea level, less at altitude, and slips once in about 250 seconds on a ladder.

How does a climber go up a ladder stood against an ice wall: clipped to what, and what holds a slip? The game climbs at 0.3 m/s at sea level and comes down at 0.9, as fast as down the rope beside it, less at altitude.
How does a climber go up a fixed rope on a jumar, on the Lhotse Face for instance: the rhythm of hand, feet and breath, and when does the second cowstail move?
How does a climber go down a fixed rope: abseiling on a belay device, with the rope wrapped round an arm, or on the carabiner alone, and where on the South route is each used?
What is the rest step, with its rhythm of steps and breaths, and how does the rhythm change with altitude and with bottled oxygen?
On hard, steep ice such as the Lhotse Face, where a fixed rope is in place: how are the crampons placed, on the front points or flat-footed, and when does the ice axe go in?

How fast does a climber walk on ground of each steepness, up and down, in crampons and with a pack, and how much slower on a ladder? The game's walking costs what Minetti et al. measured on a treadmill, read as rise over run, from 24° down to 24° up, each metre of height costing the same past that up to 60°; a climber walks on 2.2 W/kg at sea level, before the altitude and the pack take their share, and no faster than 0.7 m/s whatever they have to spare. The power, the fastest walk and the ladder speeds are fitted to the hours the sources give the Icefall, up and down, not measured.
How often does a climber slip on snow and ice of each steepness, and on a ladder? The game has no slips up to 30°, and a chance rising to once in about 50 seconds of walking at 60°.

Up to what speed can a sliding climber stop themselves with the ice axe, on snow and on hard ice, and within how many seconds of the slip? How far from the body does the axe reach, and how hard do snow and hard ice hold a sliding climber without it? The game stops a slide no faster than 5 m/s, with the axe driven in within 1.5 m above the body, and never in the air; without the axe, a slide stops by itself only on ground gentler than about 19°, by the friction measured for ski fabrics on snow.

How much slower on the Icefall's ladders and fixed ropes is a client who has never used crampons, a jumar or a ladder than one with alpine climbs behind them, and how much faster one who has climbed a 7,000 m or an 8,000 m peak? Do they slip more, or less, for each metre? The game fits their speed there to the spread of the sources' hours for a first crossing, and leaves their slips for each metre as they are: experience brings more summits, not fewer deaths.
